messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

message.content:
**Freezing point of water at 10 kPa**

| Pressure | Approximate freezing point |
|----------|----------------------------|
| **10 kPa** | **≈ 0 °C (273.15 K)** |

---

### Why the change is almost nil  

Water’s solid‑liquid equilibrium curve (the “melting” line) has an extremely steep slope in the \(P\)-\(T\) plane:

\[
\frac{dP}{dT}\;\approx\;
\frac{\Delta H_{\text{fus}}}
      {T\,\Delta V_{m}}
   \;\sim\;4\times10^{8}\ {\rm Pa\,K^{-1}}\quad(\text{at }0^\circ\mathrm C)
\]

where  
• \(\Delta H_{\text{fus}}\) – enthalpy of fusion (\(≈333.5\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}\))  
• \(\Delta V_m\) – molar volume change upon freezing (\(≈3\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3\!\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\))

Inverting gives

\[
\frac{dT}{dP}\;\approx\;2.5\times10^{-9}\ {\rm K\,Pa^{-1}}
\]

A drop from atmospheric pressure (≈101 kPa) to 10 kPa changes the pressure by only ≈90 kPa, shifting the freezing point by

\[
\Delta T \approx 2.5\times10^{-9}\times 9\times10^{4}\ \text{K}
          \approx 2\times10^{-4}\ ^\circ\mathrm C .
\]

That is far smaller than experimental uncertainty—essentially *no measurable effect*. Thus, even at 10 kPa the freezing point stays practically at 0 °C.

> **Bottom line:** Under normal laboratory conditions, water freezes at roughly 0 °C regardless of whether the ambient pressure is 10 kPa, 20 kPa, or 101 kPa.
